October 21, 1915. 
Mr. Alexander C. Downey may be appointed a clerk in the competitive 
classified service of the Treasury Department without compliance with the 
civil-service rules. Mr. Downey has served since September 2, 1913, in the 
excepted position of private secretary to the Comptroller of the Treasury. In 
addition to the duties of private secretary it appears that Mr. Downey has 
been engaged on the work of passing upon the contracts of Army officers, which 
is considered very complicated work. The Auditor for the War Department 
states that he is in great need of a clerk capable of auditing the contracts 
of Army officers and believes that Mr. Downey's experience in the Comptroller’s 
office in similar duties eminently qualifies him to perform this work. This 
order ‘is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, the 
Civil Service Commission concurring because of testimony as to Mr. Downey’s 
special training. 
October 26, 1915. 
The following-named persons who were formerly employees of the United 
States Commission on Industrial Relations may be appointed to positions in : 
the competitive classified service without reference to the civil-service rules: 
William L. Soleau, Mary R. Burr, Adelaide L. Patrick, Mayme M. Davidson, 
Elizabeth A. Hyde, Florence Rimsnicer, Elizabeth G. Simmons, Thomas J. 
Eagan, Josephine M. Jones, Nelle B. Curry, Aloysius A. Bauer, Charles J. 
Stowell, Florence A. Cooke, Minetta Hargraves, Effie M. Nelson, Inez L. Bowser, 
Estelle Johnson, Margie N. Conner, Catherine M. Etter, Rosamond G. Krueger. 
This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Commission on In￾dustrial Relations. In a resolution unanimously adopted by the commission 
on August 11, 1915, it is stated that the employees named have been excep￾tionally faithful, that they discharged their duties with marked ability, and 
have thus shown their fitness in a practical way for employment in the classi￾fied civil service of the United States. The Civil Service Commission does 
not concur in the recommendation. 
October 28, 1915. 
Mrs. Frederick Gillman may be appointed as seamstress or flagmaker at the 
navy yard, Mare Island, Cal.,, without reference to the civil-service rules or 
navy yard regulations. Mrs. Gillman’s husband was a gunner on the submarine 
F-}, which was lost in Honolulu Harbor, and she has a child 12 years of age 
to support. This order is recommended by the Secretary of the Navy with the 
concurrence of the Civil Service Commission. 
November 16, 1915. 
Mr. Charles Hardin may be reinstated as a clerk at not to exceed $1,200 per 
annum in the Post Office Department without regard to the length of his sepa￾ration from the service. Mr. Hardin was appointed August 15, 1887, through 
appropriate examination as a clerk at $900 in the Post Office Department at 
Washington, and was removed from the position of clerk, class 8 ($1,600), on 
January 26, 1901, for irregularities in connection with the dead-letter sale. 
The records of the department show that Mr. Hardin's removal was based on 
the report and recommendation of a post-office inspector who investigated the 
charges. The Postmaster General reports that this report, which it is under￾stood was favorable to Mr. Hardin, was apparently extracted from the files by 
the previous administration. He further states that as it is believed that the 
removal of Mr. Hardin, and the manner by which he was removed, was unjust 
to him, the department feels that it would be in the interest of justice to rein￾state him. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of 
an order in this case. 
December 1, 1915. 
Mr. Lawrence A. Baker may be appointed a clerk in the competitive class of 
the Post Office Department without examination. The Civil Service Commission 
concurs in the recommendation of the Postmaster General for the appointment. 
The Postmaster General states that for the past three years the department has 
been engaged in a campaign of reorganizing post offices to systematize and stand-

The Attorney General recommends the reinstatement of Mr. Wagner because of the difficulty experienced in obtaining stenographers and typewriters who also have a knowledge of law. In view of the fact that Mr. Wagner was twice appointed through competitive examination, served for nearly four years in the classified service and for over two years in unclassified positions with a good record, the Civil Service Com- mission concurs in recommending the issuance of an order which involves merely the waiving of the year limit upon eligibility. January 21, 1915. 
Mr. James Hands, an unclassified laborer at $660 per annum in the office of the super- intendent of the State, War, and Navy Department Building, may be promoted to the position of classified laborer at $840 per annum in said office, without reference to civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy, who states that he is informed by the superintendent that on account of the special experi- ence in electrical work gained by Mr. Hands since his employment in August, 1906, he is better qualified to perform the duties of the position of skilled laborer than an eligible who would be secured from the skilled-laborer register of the Civil Service Commission; that he has made a study of electrical work, and in addition is familiar with the building and operation of the electrical force. The superintendent speaks in the highest terms of Mr. Hands’s record as a workman, and considers him well qualified to perform the duties of a skilled laborer assigned with the electrician as helper. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending the issuance of this order. 
February 4, 1915. 
Mr. Ralph Izard, who was dismissed from the position of Chinese inspector in the Immigration Service February 3, 1903, may be reinstated to the position of immigrant inspector in the Immigration Service, Department of Labor, without regard to the length of his separation from the service. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Labor, who states that he made a thorough investigation of the case and arrived at the conclusion that Mr. Izard was improperly dismissed from the service. fans hal Service Commission does not concur in recommending the issuance of 
this order 
February 19, 1915. 
Miss Sadie S Killeen may be appointed a clerk in the classified service of the Treasury Department without compliance with the civil service rules. Miss Killeen has served under temporary employment for more than nine months, having been appointed without examination because of her expert knowledge of the operation of a machine which was to be tested to determine its applicability to the posting of disbursing officers’ accounts in the Office of the Treasurer of the United States. The plan having proved satisfactory, Miss Killeen was retained to demon- strate and assist in introducing it. Her services have been of great value, and the installation of the machines has resulted in a large saving in expenses. The Civil Service Commission therefore concurs with the Secretary of the Treasury in recom- mending this order. 
February 27, 1915. 
Mr. Charles 3 O’Neill, a messenger in the Pension Office at $840 per annum, may be Promoied to a clerkship in the Pension Office without reference to the civil service rules Mr. O’Neill has been employed in the Pension Office since June 15, 1893, and has 
rendered faithful and efficient service during that time; he is performing with entire satisfaction duties ordinarily performed by clerks at $900 to $1,600 per annum. The Secretary of the Interior states that if Mr. O'Neill is rendered eligible for pro- motion, he 4 take pleasure in approving any recommendation looking to his ad￾vancement. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend this order. 
March 23, 1915. 
The year limit upon eligibilit X for reinstatement is hereby waived to permit the reinstatement of Dr. Edward P. Beverly as a physician in the Panama Canal service.

EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 123 
Dr. Beverley’s reinstatement by Executive order is recommended by Gen. George W. Goethals, Governor of the Panama Canal. Dr. Beverley entered the service on July 6, 1904; served through the period when tropical diseases were prevalent, and by his efficient service was successively promoted until he held one of the highest positions therein at the close of his service December 15, 1913, being rated as ‘‘excel- lent” in both conduct and character of work. Necessity for a change of climate required his resignation, but he has recovered from the effects of his long residence in the Tropics and desires to return to work on the Isthmus. 
The Civil Service Commission concurs in recommending this order. 
March 23, 1915. 
Edward D. White may be reinstated as a letter carrier in the Oakland, Cal., post office without regard to the length of time he has been separated from the service. He was appointed substitute carrier in the Oakland office on September 1, 1902; was made a regular carrier on October 1, 1903, and served until January 31, 1913. The Postmaster General states that as Mr. White is intelligent and was a very competent and faithful employee while in the service, the department will not interpose any objection to his reinstatement in the service. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of this order. 
April 6, 1915. 
Mr. John D. Campbell may be reinstated to a position in the Railway Mail Service without regard to the length of time he has been separated from the service. Mr. Campbell was appointed a clerk in the Railway Mail Service on October 29, 1887, classified with that service on May 1, 1889, as a clerk at $1,000 per annum, and resigned November 3, 1902, on account of his impaired physical condition. Itappears that he has now fully recovered his health. The Postmaster General states that his 
services were satisfactory to the department during his 15 years’ service and that the department will interpose no objection to his reinstatement through the issuance of an Executive order. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend this order. 
April 13, 1915. : 
Mrs. Eleanor S. Ramsay may be transferred from the position of office helper in the Government Printing Office to a clerical position in the Navy Department without reference to the civil-service rules. REPORT OF UNITED STATES CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 147 
In view of the facts the Secretary of Commerce and Labor recommends the appoint￾ment of Mrs. Hampton. 
The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation for an 
Executive order. 
June 11, 1912. 
Mrs. May Stanley may be appointed to a position in the classified service without examination under the civil-service rules. Mrs. Stanley is the widow of Will H. Stanley, superintendent of the Soboba Indian School, California, who was murdered May 3, 1912, by an Indian under the juris- diction of that superintendency. Mr. Stanley left two dependent children. Mrs. Stanley has been employed for several years in excepted positions in the Indian Service. She attended Dickinson County High School, Kansas, the Lebanon Val- ley College, Pennsylvania, and the University of Kansas, and the department believes that she will render efficient service in the capacity of teacher. In view of the facts the Civil Service Commission joins with the department in recommending the issuance of an Executive order. 
June 15, 1912. 
Mr. Oscar Wenderoth may be reinstated in the classified service to the position of Supervising Architect without regard to the length of time that he has been sepa- rated from the service. 
Mr. Wenderoth served as senior architectural draftsman and foreman of construction - in and under the Office of the Supervising Architect, from March 8, 1897, when he was appointed through appropriate examination, to April 16, 1900, when he resigned; and again from March 10, 1903, when he was reinstated by Executive order as senior architectural draftsman, to July 31, 1904. 
In view of his previous service, his experience, and his proved efficiency, the commission joins with the Secretary of the Treasury in recommending this order. 
June 19, 1912. 
Mr. M. M. Dodge may be transferred, before the completion of his probationary 
period, from the position of clerk in the War Department to naturalization examiner at Pittsburgh, Pa. : 
The transfer of Mr. Dodge was desired by the department because of his high edu- cational attainments, mature judgment, and experience in law and in administrative matters. Mr. Dodge is regarded by the Division of Naturalization as peculiarly fitted for the duties of the position at Pittsburgh to which he is to be transferred. Under the civil-service rules an employee is not eligible for transfer from one depart- ment to another until he has served for six months and has received absolute appoint￾ment, and the Civil Service Commission was unable to concur with the department in the recommendation for an Executive order. 
June 19, 1912. 
Mr. John G. Lerch may be Spoil without examination as private secretary to Mr. lugene G. Hay, member of the Board of General Appraisers. The position is one of a highly confidential nature, as the secretary to the general appraiser must of necessity know in many instances in advance of the promulgation of decisions what the decisions will be. 
Mr. Lerch has had considerable previous experience in the capacity of secretary and has passed the civil-service examination in stenography and typewriting. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation for an Executive order. 
July 10, 1912. 
Mr. Leroy A. McGee may be reinstated to the position of post-office inspector without reference to the time limit upon eligibility for reinstatement. 
Mr. McGee served for four years as a teacher in the Indian Service, for three years as a clerk in the Office of the Auditor for the Post Office Department, and three years as a post-office inspector, resigning from the latter position on October 7, 1910. He has passed the teacher examination, the post-office inspector examination, and the immigrant inspector examination with good ratings. The chief post-office inspector reports that he was a good inspector, that his work was satisfactory, that there is nothing in the files which would be considered against his reinstatement, and that since his resignation Mr. McGee has been practicing law. In view of his good record and the fact that his experience since leaving the service has been such as to increase his efficiency, the Civil Service Commission joins with the Postmaster General in recom- mending the reinstatement,

July 12, 1912. 
The following-named employees of the Tariff Board who have been especially recom- mended for retention in the public service may be transferred or appointed to appro- riate positions in the competitive classified service with the approval of the Civil A, Commission; but in the case of any such person who has not a competitive status or who has not passed an appropriate examination for the position to which 
appointment is proposed the Civil Service Commission may apply such tests of fitness as 1t deems necessary before approval: Mr. Leo Rullmann, Mrs. B. C. Woodford, Mr. Herve W. Kitzmiller, Mrs. Rose R. Aydelotte, Miss Anna E. Hutchinson, Mrs. Max West, Mr. N. I. Stone, Miss Mary E. Bishop, Mr. A. L. Colton, Mr. J. L. F. Ingold, Mr. James Otey, Mr. Wilson Evans, Mr. Travers Pinn, Mr. J. Garfield Harris. Eligibility under this order shall cease at the expiration of one year from the date of the person’s separation from the Tariff Board. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the chairman of the Tariff Board, with the approval of the Civil Service Commission, on account of the faithful and meritorious service of the employees, most of whom have had considerable experience in the Government service, although not in all cases in the classified service, but in - no case less than 18 months. 
July 19, 1912. 
Mr. Dorsey E. Phillips, of Missouri, may be appointed to a clerical position in the competitive classified service without reference to the civil-service rules. Mr. Phillips served for five years in the Regular Army prior to May 30, 1898. He passed the clerk examination held at St. Joseph, Mo., on March 22, 1909, with a rating of 78.35 and was temporarily employed as a result of this examination from October 25, 1909, to Feb- ruary 18, 1910. He also passed the census-clerk examination with a rating of 80.25, as a result of which he received appointment in the Bureau of the Census and served from September 6, 1910, to February 29, 1912, when he was separated on account of a necessary reduction of force. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the approval of this order.

April 25, 1907.
Frederick L. Dunlap, of the State of Michigan, may be appointed to the posi¬
tion of associate chemist and member of the food and drug inspection in the
classified service of the Department of Agriculture without examination and
certification by the Civil Service Commission.
The execution of the food and drugs act required a large additional force of
chemists and inspectors to be added to the Bureau of Chemistry of the Depart¬
ment of Agriculture. It became necessary to create a board to find facts with
regard to the correct labeling of drugs and food products under the law. In
creating this board it was thought wise to bring into the Department a chemist
of first-class basic training and high standing in his profession, who, under the
authority of the Chief of the Bureau of Chemistry, should take part in original
investigation and in the examination and handling of correspondence touching
the topics under consideration. After correspondence with the presidents of
leading universities, Dr. Frederick L. Dunlap, of the University of Michigan,
was selected by the Secretary of Agriculture for the appointment.
April 29, 1907.
Harrison L. Deam, a veteran of the civil war, who has served satisfactorily as
a watchman in the Department of the Interior under temporary appointment,
may be permanently appointed a watchman without reference to the civil￾service rules.
Mr. Deam enlisted as a private on August 12, 1S61, and after passing through
various grades was mustered out of the service January 10, 1866, as a major.
He was temporarily employed for some time in the Interior Department as a
watchman and was found to be well qualified for that position. He is 69 shears
of age, strong, and in good health.
April 30, 1907.
Mr. Nathaniel C. Murray, now a special field agent in the Bureau of Statistics
in the Department of Agriculture, may be appointed assistant statistician in
the classified service in the Department of Agriculture without compliance with
the civil-service rules.
The Secretary of Agriculture recommended the action taken in this case on
the ground that Mr. Murray, who was an unclassified agent in the Bureau of
Statistics, was thoroughly qualified by training and experience to perform the
duties of assistant statistician. It was desired to utilize his services during
the absence of the statistician in connection with the Cuban census.
April 30, 1907.
Miss Elsie E. Lower, of the State of Pennsylvania, a student assistant in the
Department of Agriculture, may be appointed a clerk and artist in the classified
service .of the Department of Agriculture without examination and certification
by the Civil Service Commission.
Miss Lower was appointed a student assistant in the Department of Agricul¬
ture June 29, 1900, at a salai*y of $300. She is in reality an artist who paints
pictures of fruits, flowers, grain, nuts, and other plant life for reproduction in
the publications of the Depai’tment. She has made a specialty of this kind of
work and is very talented in it. She had not the general education and quali¬
fications for passing the examination and therefore could not be promoted
above the salary of $300 without an Executive order, and it was thought un¬
fair to continxxe her at this meager salary in view of the service which she
was rendering. She is the daughter of an old soldier and a medal-of-honor man.
April 30, 1907.
Mi*. James D. Rowan, jr., of the State of Iowa, and Mr. Charles L. Gooch, of
the District of Columbia, now student assistants in the Bureau of Plant Indus¬
try in the Department of Agriculture, may each be appointed a gardener in

Mr. William Grant, of the State of Iowa, now a student assistant in the
office of public roads in the Department of Agriculture, may be appointed a
laboratory helper in the Department of Agriculture upon passing a noncom¬
petitive examination by the Civil Service Commission for laboratory helper in

Mr. Rowan was appointed student assistant in the Bureau of Plant Industry
on April 25, 1904, at a salary of $300 per annum, and Mr. Gooch was appointed
to a similar position on May 23, 1903. The Secretary of Agriculture wrote to
the President stating that these men had been employed in the pathological and
physiological greenhouses, where they developed such aptitude in that special
line of work that it would be unfortunate for the Department to lose their
services and have to train others in their places. lie therefore requested au¬
thority for their noncompetitive examination as gardeners in order that their
salaries might be increased.
Mr. Grant was appointed as a student assistant in the office of public roads
February 25, 1904, at a salary of $300 per annum. He has served continuously
in the testing and chemical laboratories and has rendered such satisfactory
service and evidenced such capacity and aptitude as a laboratory helper as to
justify his transfer to a position of that grade.
These three student assistants and Miss Elsie E. Lower, for whose classifica¬
tion an Executive order was promulgated on the same date, constitute the force
of student assistants in the Department employed in Washington, and it was
stated that it was not intended to appoint any more student assistants for
service at Washington, D. C.

Claude I. Parker, of Louisiana, may be appointed librarian for the law library
or to a clerical position in the General Land Office.
Mr. Parker was a clerk in the Bureau of Forestry, a law student, and a
young man of energy and experience whom the Commissioner of the General
Land Office considered well qualified for the position. He could not be trans¬
ferred by reason of the statutory limitation requiring three years’ service in
one Department before transfer to another. The action was recommended by
the Secretary of the Interior.

June 30, 1916. 
Mr. Warren J. Brown, Mr. Henry C. Mansfield, and Mrs. Florence E. Cleve￾land may be appointed as clerks in the classified service of the Government with￾out reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recom￾mendation of the Secretary of War, who submits a detailed report from the 
governor of the Panama Canal giving special reasons as to why the same should 
be issued, in view of which it is believed that the appointment of these three 
persons will be in the interest of the service. From the governor’s report it ap￾pears that Messrs. Brown and Mansfield have rendered long and very satisfac￾tory service in the employment of the Government on the Isthmus of Panama; 
and that Mrs. Cleveland, whose husband was killed May 23, 1914, while em￾ployed as an operator of one of the towing locomotives of the Panama Canal, 
has been employed in an excepted position in the Panama Canal service since 
November 16, 1914, in which position it appears she has rendered very satis￾factory service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recom￾mendation. 
July 14, 1916. 
Mrs. Olivia Blanchard may be appointed to a position in the classified service 
under the Department of Labor without reference to the civil-service rules. This 
order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Labor, who states 
that the department contemplates the establishment of a branch of the United 
States Employment Service in the city of New Orleans, La., and that it is neces￾sary that a woman employee be assigned thereto to attend to applications of 
women for employment or help, and it is believed that a woman as favorably 
known in New Orleans as Mrs. Blanchard is would possess advantages calcu￾lated to promote the interests of the new employment service, and that her 
acquaintance would make her services desirable in the labors of woman’s and 
girl’s division of said service involving vocational direction as to industrial 
training of girls. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recom￾mendation. 
July 14, 1916. 
Mr. Marion T. Edwards may be appointed to the position of assistant messen￾ger qualified in the operation and repair of automobiles, in the Bureau of Stand￾ards at $720 per annum, without reference to the civil-service rules. This order 
is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce and the Direc￾tor of the Bureau of Standards, who state that the position to which it is pro￾posed to appoint Mr. Edwards is a confidential post; that by experience and 
training Mr. Edwards is especially qualified for the position; and that his ap￾pointment would be in the interests of good administration. The Civil Service 
Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
July 14, 1916. 
Miss Ruth L. O'Donnell may be appointed to a position in the Bureau of Effi￾ciency without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the 
recommendation of the Chief of the Bureau of Efficiency, who states that Miss 
O’Donnell has been employed in his office at various times during the past two 
years; that her services have been most satisfactory; and that her permanent 
appointment to the force of the Bureau of Efficiency would be a distinct advan￾tage to the bureau. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recom￾mendation. 
July 18, 1916.

temporarily as a storekeeper-gauger in that district from September, 1915, until 
June 26, 1916; that he is qualified to competently fill any position in the store￾keeper-gauger service; and that his permanent appointment will be in the inter￾est of efficient administration. The collector further states that the stress of 
work at this time in his district necessitates the employment of an experienced 
man. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treas￾ury. Mr. Smith is on the civil-service register. 
July 19, 1916. 
Mr, Arthur E. Wilson may be permanently appointed to a clerical position in 
the office of the Surgeon General, Public Health Service, without reference to

EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 133 
October 22, 1913. 
Mrs. Mary R. Geddings may be appointed to a position in the classified service with 
out reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. Mrs. Geddings is the widow of Surg. Henry D. Geddings, of the Public Health Serv- ice, who was a commissioned medical officer in that service for about 25 years, and who rendered distinguished service in matters relating to sanitation and public health. 
He also rendered valuable service in several epidemics of yellow fever at a time when few medical men were immune to that disease and its cause was but little known. The Secretary of the Treasury states that it would be a fitting testimonial to the serv- ices of Surg. Geddings to waive the civil-service rules to permit the appointment of Mrs. Geddings in the classified service. The Civil Service Commission does not 
recommend that an Executive order be issued in this case. 
October 23, 1913. 
Mr. Henry J. Cokayne may be reinstated as a mail carrier in the Postal Service without regard to the length of his separation from the service. This order is issued for the reason that Mr. Cokayne’s dismissal does not appear to have been warranted by the facts. His reinstatement is recommended by the post- office inspector who made an investigation of the case, and by the First Assistant Postmaster General. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending 
that an Executive order be issued authorizing the reinstatement of Mr. Cokayne. 
October 24, 1913. 
Mr. Solon J. Boughton may be reinstated as assistant examiner in the Patent Office, Department of the Interior, without reference to the period of his separation from the service. Mr. Boughton served as an assistant patent examiner from December 1, 1907, to August 9, 1911. He resigned for the purpose of taking up his residence in Colorado when it was found that he had contracted tuberculosis. A cure was effected within a 
short time and during his period of eligibility he communicated with the Patent Office relative to reinstatement but was ad vised to remain in Colorado and was promised that a recommendation would be made for his reinstatement when he desired to resume his duties. The Secretary of the Interior recommends the reinstatement on account of Mr. Boughton’s experience and the fact that he served with great ability. The Civil 
Service Commission concurs in recommending this Executive order. 
October 29, 1913. 
Mr. John H. Jenkins may be reinstated to the position of immigrant inspector in the Immigration Service without regard to the length of his separation from the service. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Labor, who, after a 
thorough investigation of the matter, is satisfied that Mr. Jenkins’ dismissal from the service was not warranted by the facts. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending the issuance of an Executive order in this case. 
October 29, 1913. 
William A. Ryan may be appointed to the position of comptroller (in charge of all finances and accounting) in the Reclamation Service. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Interior, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission, and is based upon Mr. Ryan’s un- usual qualifications for the position and the close personal relationship which he will bear to the Secretary of the Interior. Mr. Ryan has been in the employ of the Inter- state Commerce Commission during the past six years assigned to the duty of examining the books and accounts of transportation companies, and conducted a notable investi- gation which covered a period of three years. He is thoroughly familiar with large financial affairs, it having been his business for several years to draft the plans for the financing of great industrial corporations, and moreover he has an intimate personal knowledge of irrigation experiments and projects. He has been known to the Secre- tary of the Interior for 25 years, and knows his attitude so perfectly that he will be able to state his policies and deal with the more than 20,000 water users without 
embarrassment to the Secretary. 
October 30, 1913. 
Charles J. Brown may be reinstated as a clerk in the classified service of the Treasury Department without observance of the rules regarding reinstatement after the expira- tion of one year from date of separation from the service. This order is recommended by the Secretary of the Treasury in view of Mr. Brown's 
former efficient service in that department.

REPORT OF UNITED STATES CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 139 
The opinion of the President conveyed in the letter of his Secretary will be treated as an Executive order. (Minute 1, Mar. 23, 1912.) 
PETITIONS TO CONGRESS BY CIVIL-SERVICE EMPLOYEES, 
April 8, 1912.1 
It is hereby ordered that petitions or other communications regarding public busi- ness addressed to Congress or either House or any committee or Member thereof by officers or employees in the civil service of the United States shall be transmitted through the heads of their respective departments or offices, who shall forward them without delay with such comment as they may deem requisite in the public interest. Officers and employees are strictly prohibited either directly or indirectly from at- tempting to secure legislation, or to influence pending legislation, except in the manner above prescribed. This order supersedes the Executive orders of January 31, 1902, January 25, 1906, and November 26, 1909, regarding the same general matter 
EXCEPTIONS IN MACHINE SHOP OF THE BUREAU OF THE CENSUS. 
August 21, 1812. - 
With a view to meeting emergencies in the machine shop of the Bureau of the Census, in connection with the continuation of the Thirteenth Decennial Census work during the fiscal year 1913, the Secretary of Commerce and Labor is hereby authorized to employ, until June 30, 1913, without reference to the civil-service rules, such machinists, toolmakers, electricians, and apprentice boys (machinists) as may be necessary for the prosecution of the work whenever, in his opinion, it is not prac- ticable to make such appointments from the civil-service lists. This order extends the authority for similar appointments contained in the Executive order of December 29, 1909. The Civil Service Commission concurs with the department in recommending this order, in view of the representations of the department as to its necessity. ! 
EMPLOYMENT IN PENSION OFFICE OF FORMER TREASURY EMPLOYEES. 
August 24, 1912. 
The Commissioner of Pensions is directed to employ as extra clerks under the appro- priation of $300,000 carried in the sundry civil act approved August 24, 1912, the 30 persons heretofore employed in the office of the Auditor for the Post Office Depart- ment whose names are on the list furnished to the President in a letter of the Secre- tary of the Treasury dated August 22, 1912, said appropriation act authorizing the Commissioner of Pensions to employ clerks heretofore employed in other departments of the Government service. All of these persons except one have a competitive classified status and will be eligible for reinstatement in the Treasury Department under the civil-service rules. 
MODERATOR OF A TOWN MEETING MAY BE A CLASSIFIED EMPLOYEE, 
August 24, 1912. 
The temporary office of moderator of a town meeting and offices of a like character are hereby excepted from the operation of the Executive order of January 17, 1873, prohibiting persons in the Federal civil service from holding office under the charter or ordinances of any municipal corporation, and may be held by persons in the execu- tive civil service. Membership in the civil service ought not to prevent an employee from taking part in the ordinary municipal affairs of the community in which he lives, where that part does not involve permanent service but only such a temporary duty as that of acting as chairman of a municipal business meeting, where such service is not compensated by any salary or other emolument, and where the attention required by such service does not interfere with the regular and efficient discharge of the duties of the Federal office held. In the exercise of the privilege granted by this order officers and employees must not neglect their official duties and must not engage in national, State, or county political activity in violation of the civil-service rules; and in seeking the local offices named or in performing the duties thereof employees shall not use the authority or influence of their Federal positions nor take an active part in political management or 
 
in political campaigns.

No such special employee now serving shall be regarded as classified hereunder or shall acquire any right of promotion or transfer under the rules unless he is specially commended therefor by the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, with the approval of the Secretary of the Treasury, because of efficient services rendered, and whose name is embraced in the is furnished to the Civil Service Commission by the Treasury Department of this 
ate. This order shall take effect October 1, 1912, and is issued with the concurrence of the Secretary of the Treasury and the Civil Service Commission. 
CLASSIFICATION AUTHORIZED OF CERTAIN EXPERTS IN THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRI- CULTURE. August 26, 1912. 
Not exceeding 115 persons appointed as experts and agents without examination under Subdivision IX, section 1 of Schedule A, of the civil-service rules, and who now are engaged upon work similar to that of competitive employees, and who are especially recommended by the Secretary of Agriculture because of their proved capacity for efficient service may be transferred to appropriate competitive positions in the Department of Agriculture. By Executive order of this date the provision of the civil-service rules permitting the appointment of agents and experts of the Department of Agriculture without examination is amended to fix more definitely the conditions under which appoint- ments can be made. This order will thus permit the classification of efficient em- ployees who can not be properly regarded as agents or experts under the amended procedure. Many of these persons are college graduates and, having been appointed at a time when agricultural colleges had not developed courses of study along certain technical lines pursued by the department, have become technologists and experts while engaged in the work of the department. The Civil Service Commission recommends this order.

146 REPORT OF UNITED STATES CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
April 22,1912. 
Having considered the written arguments for and against the application for rein- statement of Charles H. Quackenbush in the Railway Mail Service, and having 
reached a conclusion that the offense for which Mr. Quackenbush was removed does not merit more of a penalty than a suspension without pay for a year, and that such penalty has been satisfied, I hereby direct that Mr. Quackenbush may be reinstated in the Railway Mail Service without reference to the provisions of the civil-service rule governing reinstatements. This order 1s made without the approval or disapproval of the Civil Service Com- mission and against the recommendation of the Postmaster General. 
April 30, 1912. 
Commander Homer C. Poundstone, United States Navy, retired, may be employed on the rolls of the United States Civil Service Commission without examination under the civil-service rules. This action is taken at the request of the Civil Service Commission because of his peculiar and exceptional qualifications and his high and recognized attainments. 
May 10, 1912. 
Miss Louise Lester may be appointed a clerk in the classified executive civil service without compliance with the civil-service rules. This order is issued for the reason that it is recommended by the Secretary of the Treasury so that Miss Lester may be appointed a special witness of the destruction of United States securities in the Treasury Department, it being the Secretary’s judgment that Miss Lester possesses special qualifications which will render her par- ticularly desirable as a member of the destruction committee. 
May 27, 1912. 
Mr. Walter L. Barnum may be reinstated to an appropriate clerical position in the classified service without regard to the length of his separation therefrom. Mr. Barnum resigned from the competitive position of clerk in the Post Office Department on February 19, 1908. Since that time he has oso the examination in stenography and typewriting with a high grade, and has eveloped the qualifica- tions of an expert clerk during his service in an excepted position in the Post Office Department from April 1, 1909, to the present time. In view of his high rating and his record as an expert clerk, the commission joins with the Postmaster General in recommending the order. 
May 28, 1912. 
Mr. Wesley M. Featherly, a deputy collector of customs in the Key West, Fla., district from January 1, 1898, to August 21, 1899, when he resigned, may be reinstated without reference to the year limit of the civil-service rules. 
The Civil Service Commission not being advised of the reasons for excepting Mr. Featherly from the year limitation fixed by the civil-service rules makes no recom- mendation respecting this order. 
June 5, 1912. 
Mr. Arthur S. Blum may be reinstated as photographer in the Forest Service, Washington, D. C., without regard to the length of his separation from the service. The Civil Service Commission joins the Secretary of Agriculture in recommending this order because of the unfair treatment received by Mr. Blum through the mis- statements of his superior officer, who has since been adjudged insane. 
June 6, 1912. 
Mrs. Margaret A. Hampton, a clerk at $1,000 per annum on the temporary force of the Thirteenth Census, may be appointed as a clerk at $1,000 per annum in the classified service. 
Mrs. Hampton was appointed through appropriate examination with a rating of 77.45, as a clerk at $600 per annum on the temporary force of the Thirteenth Decennial Census on April 1, 1910, and by successive promotions reached her present rate of $1,000 per annum. She has twice passed the departmental clerk examination. On 
June 24, 1910, while leaving the Census Building, she lost her balance and pitched head first down the full flight of stairs, her skirt having caught on one of the iron plates of the stairs, sustaining injuries which necessitated her absence from the office until July 13 and again from September 30 until December 4. There is grave doubt whether she will ever recover her health, according to statements of several physicians who have attended her. The bureau has endeavored to make all possible restitution but, under existing law, she can not be retained beyond June 30, 1912. Notwith- standing the accident her value as a clerk is above the average.

REPORT OF UNITED STATES CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 147 
In view of the facts the Secretary of Commerce and Labor recommends the appoint￾ment of Mrs. Hampton. 
The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation for an 
Executive order. 
June 11, 1912. 
Mrs. May Stanley may be appointed to a position in the classified service without examination under the civil-service rules. Mrs. Stanley is the widow of Will H. Stanley, superintendent of the Soboba Indian School, California, who was murdered May 3, 1912, by an Indian under the juris- diction of that superintendency. Mr. Stanley left two dependent children. Mrs. Stanley has been employed for several years in excepted positions in the Indian Service. She attended Dickinson County High School, Kansas, the Lebanon Val- ley College, Pennsylvania, and the University of Kansas, and the department believes that she will render efficient service in the capacity of teacher. In view of the facts the Civil Service Commission joins with the department in recommending the issuance of an Executive order. 
June 15, 1912. 
Mr. Oscar Wenderoth may be reinstated in the classified service to the position of Supervising Architect without regard to the length of time that he has been sepa- rated from the service. 
Mr. Wenderoth served as senior architectural draftsman and foreman of construction - in and under the Office of the Supervising Architect, from March 8, 1897, when he was appointed through appropriate examination, to April 16, 1900, when he resigned; and again from March 10, 1903, when he was reinstated by Executive order as senior architectural draftsman, to July 31, 1904. 
In view of his previous service, his experience, and his proved efficiency, the commission joins with the Secretary of the Treasury in recommending this order. 
June 19, 1912. 
Mr. M. M. Dodge may be transferred, before the completion of his probationary 
period, from the position of clerk in the War Department to naturalization examiner at Pittsburgh, Pa. : 
The transfer of Mr. Dodge was desired by the department because of his high edu- cational attainments, mature judgment, and experience in law and in administrative matters. Mr. Dodge is regarded by the Division of Naturalization as peculiarly fitted for the duties of the position at Pittsburgh to which he is to be transferred. EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 123 
Dr. Beverley’s reinstatement by Executive order is recommended by Gen. George W. Goethals, Governor of the Panama Canal. Dr. Beverley entered the service on July 6, 1904; served through the period when tropical diseases were prevalent, and by his efficient service was successively promoted until he held one of the highest positions therein at the close of his service December 15, 1913, being rated as ‘‘excel- lent” in both conduct and character of work. Necessity for a change of climate required his resignation, but he has recovered from the effects of his long residence in the Tropics and desires to return to work on the Isthmus. 
The Civil Service Commission concurs in recommending this order. 
March 23, 1915. 
Edward D. White may be reinstated as a letter carrier in the Oakland, Cal., post office without regard to the length of time he has been separated from the service. He was appointed substitute carrier in the Oakland office on September 1, 1902; was made a regular carrier on October 1, 1903, and served until January 31, 1913. The Postmaster General states that as Mr. White is intelligent and was a very competent and faithful employee while in the service, the department will not interpose any objection to his reinstatement in the service. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of this order. 
April 6, 1915. 
Mr. John D. Campbell may be reinstated to a position in the Railway Mail Service without regard to the length of time he has been separated from the service. Mr. Campbell was appointed a clerk in the Railway Mail Service on October 29, 1887, classified with that service on May 1, 1889, as a clerk at $1,000 per annum, and resigned November 3, 1902, on account of his impaired physical condition. Itappears that he has now fully recovered his health. The Postmaster General states that his 
services were satisfactory to the department during his 15 years’ service and that the department will interpose no objection to his reinstatement through the issuance of an Executive order. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend this order. 
April 13, 1915. : 
Mrs. Eleanor S. Ramsay may be transferred from the position of office helper in the Government Printing Office to a clerical position in the Navy Department without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy, who states that Mrs. Ramsay has a very good record for efficiency in the Government Printing Office, and, after investigation, he is satisfied that she is competent to per- form satisfactorily clerical duties in the Navy Department. Mrs. Ramsay was appointed a gold worker in the Government Printing Office, September 28, 1903, and since Sobtember 20, 1907, has been continuously employed as an office helper at 35 cents per hour. ; The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending this order. 
April 17, 1915. 
Samuel Z. C. Westerfield, of Nebraska, now a messenger with the British Arbitra- tion Claims Commission, may be appointed without examination to an assistant messengership in the Department of State. The position now filled by Mr. Wester- field is abolished by legislation effective July 1, and because of his efficiency it is 
deemed in the interest of the public service to continue him in the employ of the Department of State. 
April 21, 1915. 
Mr. Arthur S. Kellom, formerly a letter carrier at the Chico, Cal., post office, may be reinstated in the postal service without regard to the length of time he has been separated from the service. ‘he reinstatement of Mr. Kellom is recommended by the Postmaster General, who states that a careful review of the papers in this case discloses that the charges on which the carrier was removed were not wholly true and that the action taken by the department was based upon statements which for the most part are not borne out by facts recently developed and were the result of prejudice on the part of the former ostmaster and, possibly, the post-office inspector who conducted the case, and it 18 believed that an injustice was done and that the offenses charged against Carrier Eolloms even if true, were not such as to justify so severe a punishment as that inflicted.

April 23, 1915. 
Fred Gilmore, of the District of Columbia, and Robert Taylor, of the District of Columbia, unclassified laborers at $660 per annum in the Post Office Department, may be appointed classified laborers at $660 per annum in the same department without reference to civil-service rules. The above order was issued on request of the Postmaster General, who stated that these men were highly desirable as messengers, entirely trustworthy, and had rendered excellent service, having been directly connected with the office of the Postmaster General since the beginning of the present administration. 
April 27, 1915. 
Mr. Charles W. G. Brett may be transferred from the position of mechanician at 
$1,200 per annum to a clerkship at the same salary, in the Bureau of the Census, Department of Commerce, without reference to the civil-service rules. Mr. Brett was appointed as mechanician on September 16, 1908. On March 19, 1912, he met with an accident, in the line of duty, which resulted in the loss of his left eye. His transfer to the clerical rollisrecommended by the Director of the Census, who states that Mr. Brett’s experience in connection with the various machines used in the bureau, his familiarity with the matter to be tabulated, and his general educa- tion are believed to be such as to fit him for clerical duties, and that his services have always been satisfactory. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
April 27, 1915. 
Mrs. Lillian B. S. Grant may be reinstated to a position in the classified service in the Post Office Department without regard to the length of time she has been sep- arated from the service. Mrs. Grant, as Mrs. Lillie B. Silcott, was appointed to the position of printer’s assistant in the Bureau of Printing and Engraving on August 2, 1895, and was pro- moted to operative and through the several grades of that position. On July 1, 1902, she was transferred to the Post Office Department as clerk at $900, and was promoted to $1,000 July 1, 1905. She resigned May 9, 1912. 
The Postmaster General advises that it is stated that Mrs. Grant’s husband is a ermanent invalid, and that she is therefore compelled to provide a livelihood for Poth her husband and herself.
